evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Universal jamming grippers function through two distinct operational states: a relaxed atmospheric state allowing passive geometric adaptation to objects, and an evacuated jammed state where granular particle compaction induces petrification and stiffness increase to retain grasped objects.

Grasp engagement and retention in universal jamming grippers depend on three distinct physical mechanisms: static friction forces at microscopic contact interfaces, geometric constraints providing normal retention forces, and vacuum chambers creating suction pressure differentials.

Membrane wall thickness strongly modulates grasp friction: a thin latex envelope (0.15 mm) transmits internal granular morphology to the external surface to create macroscopic waviness (reaching 74.86 µm for 1.0 mm beads), whereas thicker silicone walls (1.0–2.0 mm) cushion and conceal internal particle relief.

Energy absorbed during pull-off serves as an index of grasp robustness against dynamic inertial forces and vibrations, scaling inversely with envelope Shore hardness among silicones and achieving peak values exceeding 10 mJ in thin latex combined with 0.3–0.4 mm glass beads.

The deformation force required during passive compression is primarily governed by envelope membrane elasticity and thickness rather than grain size alone, with Shore 00-10 silicone exhibiting near-zero deformation force while Shore A-25 exceeded 20 N.

experimental_setup: Custom universal jamming gripper prototypes comprising a rigid upper mount with an integrated air filter and hermetic sealing lip, connected to a soft conical envelope filled with glass beads
Tensile force testing machine with vertical position control and a load cell with a maximum capacity of 0.5 kN recording force-displacement curves

Custom mushroom-shaped test specimen 3D-printed from PA12 nylon using Multi Jet Fusion (linear roughness 78 µm), featuring a convex top to eliminate vacuum cup suction and an undercut defining angle φ and Region A to assess compliance to geometric constraints
Pneumatic vacuum generation line consisting of an air compressor (6–8 bar) coupled to a Venturi ejector supplying at least 0.8 bar negative pressure
Optical microscope at 20x zoom magnification to inspect granular bead sizes and verify absence of significant polydispersity
Contact surface waviness measuring device using a cut-off wavelength λ = 0.8 mm

Investigating the combined interaction of inner envelope surface roughness and granular bead size on deformation resistance
independent_variables: Granular bead diameter (4 size ranges: 0.2–0.3 mm, 0.3–0.4 mm, 0.5–0.75 mm, and 1.0 mm glass balls)
Envelope material type and corresponding minimum wall thickness (Latex at 0.15 mm, Silicone Shore 00-10 at 2.0 mm, Silicone Shore 00-50 at 2.0 mm, and Silicone Shore A-25 at 1.0 mm)
limitations_inferred: Confounding between elastomer material composition and wall thickness: latex prototypes were an order of magnitude thinner (0.15 mm) than silicone prototypes (1.0–2.0 mm), making it impossible to separate polymer mechanical properties from structural thickness effects.

Testing was restricted entirely to quasi-static, purely vertical traction (20 mm/min) against a single rigid geometry, without evaluating off-axis, shear, torsional, or high-speed dynamic manipulations.
Wear resistance, fatigue life, and puncture vulnerability of the thin latex membrane under repetitive cycling were hypothesized but not experimentally characterized.
The 153 mL filler volume and 45 mm compression limit are specific to the tested conical geometry and aspect ratio, limiting direct generalization to other envelope geometries.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Envelope wall thickness was constrained by manufacturing techniques (dip molding for latex vs. cast molding for silicones), precluding thickness variation testing within the same elastomer.
The effect of varying vacuum pressure levels was not investigated; a single constant negative pressure of 0.8 bar was utilized throughout.
Polydispersity effects arising from particle size distributions were excluded from the experimental scope.
The gripper remains purely passive with a single non-discretized actuation chamber.
The prototypes lack integrated tactile sensors, real-time sensing feedback, and closed-loop grasping control.
Testing was conducted exclusively against a single standardized PA12 mushroom-shaped specimen.
main_results: Latex envelopes achieved more than double the maximum lifted weight of silicone envelopes (reaching ~5 N), with maximum capacity occurring when combined with 1.0 mm glass beads (waviness of 74.86 µm).

Silicone prototypes exhibited minor waviness variation across all particle sizes due to wall cushioning (1.0–2.0 mm thickness), showing no clear trend between particle diameter and lifted weight, with peak silicone performance around 0.3–0.4 mm beads.

Stored detachment energy showed an inverse correlation with elastomer hardness; softer Shore 00-10 silicone absorbed nearly three times more energy than harder silicones, while latex achieved the highest energy absorption (>10 mJ for 0.3–0.4 mm beads) by maximizing both lifted force and gripping engagement distance.

Passive deformation force was dominated by membrane stiffness: the stiffest silicone (Shore A-25) required over 20 N of compression force, while the softest silicone (Shore 00-10) adapted with near-zero force; latex and Shore 00-50 required 5 to 10 N.

Granulate size did not show a clear monotonic relationship with deformation force across all envelopes, demonstrating that particle rearrangement resistance is coupled with envelope boundary tension and inner surface interaction.
modeling_methods: Simplified analytical formulation relating stored energy to maximum lifted weight and gripping distance (E = Fd)
CAD-based geometric volume calculation (153 mL theoretical interior cavity)
performance_metrics: Lifted weight / maximum tensile pull-off force (N)
Stored energy / energy absorbed during pull-off detachment (mJ)
Deformation force / steady-state compression force required for shape adaptation (N)
Gripping distance / engagement length along the specimen spherical profile (mm)
Membrane surface waviness under vacuum at cut-off λ = 0.8 mm (µm)
possible_gap_implications: The finding that thin membrane walls permit internal particle texture to emerge externally points toward developing micro-molded or composite thin-walled elastomers that combine industrial wear/tear resistance with granulate-enhanced surface friction.

The decoupling between passive deformation force (governed by envelope membrane compliance) and retention force (governed by surface waviness and jammed stiffness) indicates that jamming grippers can be customized to delicately grasp fragile items with near-zero contact force while preserving high pull-off retention.

The non-monotonic behavior observed across granulate sizes (particularly performance drops for 0.5–0.75 mm beads) highlights a need for micromechanical contact models coupling discrete particle rearrangement with elastic membrane boundaries.
paper.research_objective: To experimentally evaluate and optimize combinations of four granular filler particle diameters and four flexible envelope materials for universal jamming grippers under a simulated robotic grasping cycle (unclamped compression, vacuum jamming, and tensile traction) to establish material selection guidelines.
paper.research_problem: Industrial robots operating in unstructured or chaotic scenarios (e.g., bin picking with parts exhibiting vertical or coplanar overlap and unstable positions) struggle to grasp parts individually and reliably, while existing universal jamming gripper studies typically evaluate granular fillers and envelope membranes separately or under compressive/bending stresses rather than under realistic robotic gripping cycles involving lax compression and jammed tensile traction.

stiffness_mechanism: jamming effect / granular jamming (jamming of granular material)
paper.title: Universal Jamming Gripper: Experimental Analysis on Envelope and Granular Materials
